After the tool returns, confirm the specific result (title, id, or new status) in one short natural sentence, never copying scenario metadata or fabricating fields the schema or user did not provide.
reasoner.101: When reasoning about a task-management request, first classify the intent as either task creation or status update, then extract exactly the arguments the user named (title for creation; identifier and new status for updates) and plan a single tool call with that minimal payload. If the identifier or status value is genuinely ambiguous after checking prior turns, ask one specific, targeted question naming the missing field rather than a generic request for more details.
reasoner.102: When reasoning about a task-management request, explicitly walk through three checkpoints before acting: (1) what concrete action the customer wants (create versus status change), (2) which exact arguments they have already supplied across all prior turns, and (3) whether any required schema field is still genuinely missing. reasoner.109: When orchestrating a task-management dialog, simulate the edge case where each assumption fails before dispatching: ask what happens if the intent verb is misread, if a referenced identifier from prior turns is stale or ambiguous, or if a status value does not match the allowed enum, and only proceed when each risk is ruled out by quoted evidence. verifier.100: Before finalizing any turn in a task-management dialog, run a verifier pass that adversarially challenges your planned action: invert the intent classification and check whether the opposite verb (update instead of create, or vice versa) fits the customer's literal wording better, and test whether your chosen arguments survive a "quote-or-drop" rule where any field lacking a direct quote from the user or prior turns must be removed.
